1: # Jonah 01, 1-17
2: 
3: Open your Bibles this morning to the book of Jonah. We are beginning a study of this small but immensely powerful prophecy. Now, when most people think of Jonah, they immediately think of a large fish—a whale, as it’s often called in children’s books. They think of a sea monster and a man swallowed whole. But, church, I want to tell you at the outset: this book is not primarily about a fish. It is about God. It is about the sovereignty of God, the mercy of God, and the tragic rebellion of a man who should have known better.
4: 
5: Jonah is unique among the Minor Prophets because it is not a collection of oracles, but a narrative. It is a biography of a bi-vocational prophet from Gath-hepher in Galilee. We know from 2 Kings 14:25 that Jonah was a successful prophet who predicted the expansion of Israel's borders under Jeroboam II. He was a patriot. He was a hero in Israel. But here, in this book, we see the dark side of his heart.
6: 
7: Let’s look at verse 1: **"Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.'"**
8: 
9: This is a standard prophetic commission. The "word of the Lord" (*way-ye-hi de-bar Yah-weh* [vay-yeh-HEE deh-BAR yah-WEH]) came to him. God is the sovereign initiator. And the command is clear: "Arise" and "Go." The destination was Nineveh. Now, you have to understand, folks, Nineveh was the capital of the Assyrian Empire. These were the most brutal, bloodthirsty people in the ancient world. They were known for skinning their enemies alive and piling their skulls in heaps. They were the terrorists of the eighth century B.C.
10: 
11: And God says to Jonah, "Go and call out against it." This was a message of judgment, but inherent in every message of judgment is a window for repentance. And that is exactly what Jonah didn’t want. He didn’t want Nineveh to repent. He wanted them incinerated.
12: 
13: Look at verse 3. This is one of the saddest verses in all of Scripture: **"But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord."**
14: 
15: Notice the word "But." God said "Arise," and Jonah "rose"—but not to obey. He rose to flee (*lib-ro-ah* [liv-RO-akh]). He went the opposite direction. Nineveh was 500 miles to the east; Tarshish was 2,500 miles to the west, on the edge of the known world, in what we now know as Spain. Jonah was trying to get as far away from the land of Israel as he possibly could.
16: 
17: Why? The text says it twice: "from the presence of the Lord." Now, Jonah was a theologian. He knew Psalm 139. He knew he couldn't actually hide from God's Spirit. What he was fleeing was the *localized* presence of God in the land and the *service* of God as His prophet. He was resigning his commission. He was saying, "I’m done with You, Lord, if this is what You require."
18: 
19: Folks, let me tell you something: Sin always leads "down." Notice the repetition in verse 3. He "went down" to Joppa. He "went down" into the ship. Later in verse 5, he goes "down" into the hold. Eventually, he goes "down" into the sea and "down" into the belly of the fish. When you walk away from the presence of the Lord, your life enters a terminal downward trajectory. You may think you are finding freedom, but you are only finding the depths.
20: 
21: But look at verse 4. God does not let His children go that easily. **"But the Lord hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up."**
22: 
23: The Hebrew word for "hurled" is *tul* (טּוּל). It’s a violent word. It’s the word you’d use for throwing a spear. God threw a storm at the ship. Church, this is the "hound of heaven" in action. This is the severe mercy of God. He loves Jonah too much to let him succeed in his rebellion. If you are a child of God and you are running from Him today, expect a storm. It is the most loving thing God can do—to wreck your ship to save your soul.
24: 
25: In verse 5, we see the reaction of the sailors: **"Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god."** These were seasoned sailors, men of the sea, and they were terrified. This wasn't a normal storm; it was a supernatural "tempest" (*sa-ar* [SAH-ar]). They began "hurling" their cargo into the sea. They were doing everything humanly possible to save themselves.
26: 
27: And where was the man of God? Verse 5 tells us: **"But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep."** 
28: 
29: This is astounding. The pagans are praying, and the prophet is snoring. Jonah is in a state of spiritual stupor. This is the numbness that sin produces. He has a seared conscience. He thinks he has escaped. He is so indifferent to the life of others that he can sleep while the crew is perishing because of *his* sin.
30: 
31: Church, guard your heart against this kind of apathy. When you can sin and then sleep peacefully, you are in a very dangerous place.
32: 
33: In verse 6, the pagan captain rebukes the prophet: **"What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."** Isn't that ironic? The pagan has to tell the prophet to pray. The world is calling the church to its duty.
34: 
35: Finally, the sailors decide to cast lots to find the culprit. Verse 7: **"And they said to one another, 'Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us.' So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah."** 
36: 
37: Now, we know from Proverbs 16:33 that "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord." God is sovereign over the dice. He points the finger directly at Jonah. There is no more hiding.
38: 
39: They begin to interrogate him in verse 8, asking about his occupation, his country, his people. And Jonah gives his testimony in verse 9: **"I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."**
40: 
41: Listen to that confession. It is perfectly orthodox. He identifies himself as a worshiper of *Yahweh*, the "God of heaven," the Creator of the very sea that is currently trying to kill them. But, folks, his theology was a mile high and his obedience was an inch deep. He "fears" the Lord with his lips, but he defies the Lord with his feet. This is the height of hypocrisy.
42: 
43: The sailors are "exceedingly afraid" in verse 10. They realize that they are caught in a divine crossfire. They ask him, "What shall we do to you?" (v. 11). The storm is getting worse. And Jonah gives the answer in verse 12: **"Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon us."**
44: 
45: Jonah knows the only way to satisfy the justice of God is through a sacrifice. He sentences himself to death. He doesn't want to repent and go to Nineveh; he’d rather die in the ocean. But notice the sailors’ response in verse 13. They try to save him. They "rowed hard" (*ya-kh-te-ru* [yakh-te-ROO] – literally "dug in") to get back to land. 
46: 
47: This is a picture of man’s attempt to save himself through works. They are trying to overcome God's decree with their own strength. But you can't out-row the Almighty. The sea only grew "more and more tempestuous."
48: 
49: Eventually, they realize it is futile. In verse 14, they pray to *Yahweh*. These pagans are starting to talk like believers! They ask for mercy, acknowledging that "You, O Lord, have done as it pleased you." That is a confession of divine sovereignty.
50: 
51: Verse 15: **"So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging."**
52: 
53: Immediately, there is a "great calm." The transformation was instantaneous. And what was the result? Verse 16: **"Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows."** 
54: 
55: Do you see the irony? Jonah, the runaway prophet, becomes the most successful missionary in the book so far—by accident! Even in his rebellion, God uses him to bring these pagan sailors to a state of worship and sacrifice. God will be glorified, folks, either through your obedience or in spite of your disobedience.
56: 
57: The chapter ends with verse 17: **"And the Lord appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights."**
58: 
59: The word "appointed" (*man-ah* [maw-NAW]) is key. It means God specifically prepared this creature. This wasn't a random event. It was a miracle of preservation. In the midst of the sea of judgment, God provided a submarine of mercy. 
60: 
61: And as we know from the lips of our Lord Jesus in Matthew 12, this was more than just a miracle. It was a "sign." Just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, so the Son of Man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Jonah was a type of Christ. He was "hurled" into the sea so that others might be saved. But whereas Jonah was a sinful man running from God, Jesus was the sinless Man doing the will of God, willingly being swallowed by the "sea" of God's wrath so that we—the perishing sailors—might have eternal peace.
62: 
63: As we close, let me ask you: Are you running? Are you in a "downward" trajectory? Don't wait for the storm to break the ship. Arise, call out to your God, and find the mercy that is available in the One who was swallowed by death so that you might live. Let’s pray.

5: The book of Jonah is often relegated to the realm of children's stories, remembered primarily for its "big fish." {
  "Content": "# Sermon Outline: A Heart Broken for God's Glory\n## Scripture: Nehemiah 1:1–11\n\n**Big Idea:** When God’s work lies in ruin and His name is brought into reproach, true spiritual leadership begins not with human schemes, but with a broken heart that seeks the sovereign, covenant-keeping God in repentant, promise-claiming prayer.\n\n**Anchor Point:** Verse 4—\"As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.\"\n\n---\n\n### I. The Ruin of the Remnant and the Broken Heart of the Leader (vv. 1–4)\n*   **The Setting in Susa:** \"In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel\" (v. 1).\n    *   November–December 445 B.C., during the reign of Artaxerxes I Longimanus.\n    *   Susa was the luxurious winter residence of the Persian monarchs—a place of imperial power, opulence, and personal security.\n*   **The Shepherd's Inquiry:** \"Hanani, one of my brothers, came... And I asked them concerning the Jews... and concerning Jerusalem\" (v. 2).\n    *   Though elevated in a foreign pagan court, Nehemiah’s heart was neither secularized nor indifferent; he cared deeply for God’s people and God’s city.\n*   **The Crushing Report:** \"The remnant... is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire\" (v. 3).\n    *   \"Great trouble\" (*ra'ah gedolah* [rah-AW geh-do-LAW])—acute affliction, distress, and economic misery.\n    *   \"Shame / Reproach\" (*cherpah* [kher-PAW])—disgrace in the eyes of hostile neighbors (cf. Sanballat, Tobiah); the defenselessness of Jerusalem reflected poorly upon the name and honor of Yahweh.\n    *   The wall was \"broken down\" (*meforetzet* [meh-fo-REH-tset]) and the wooden gates \"burned with fire\" (*yatzetu va'esh* [yaht-seh-TOO vah-ESH]), leaving the city vulnerable to plundering enemies.\n*   **The Agony of Intercession:** \"As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven\" (v. 4).\n    *   Nehemiah does not jump into self-reliant activism or political maneuvering.\n    *   His immediate reaction is brokenness: weeping (*ebkeh* [ev-KEH]) and prolonged mourning (*et'abbalah* [et-ahb-bah-LAW]).\n    *   He turns instinctively to \"the God of heaven\" (*Elohei ha-shamayim* [el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]), recognizing that the only remedy for spiritual devastation is divine intervention.\n\n### II. The God-Centered Approach to Prayer: Adoration and Reverence (v. 5)\n*   **The Proper Object of Worship:** \"O Lord God of heaven\" (*Yahweh Elohei ha-shamayim* [yah-WEH el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]).\n    *   Nehemiah uses the covenant name *Yahweh* combined with the transcendent title \"God of heaven\"—He who rules above every earthly potentate, including the Persian emperor.\n*   **The Majesty of His Character:** \"The great and awesome God\" (*El haggadol ve-hannora* [ALE hag-gah-DOLE ve-han-no-RAW]).\n    *   Biblical prayer begins not with man’s needs, but with God’s holiness and grandeur.\n    *   True prayer trembles before divine majesty.\n*   **The Fidelity of His Covenant:** \"Who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments\" (*shomer habberith vehachesed* [sho-MAYR hab-beh-REETH veh-ha-KHEH-sed]).\n    *   *Chesed* [KHEH-sed]—unfailing loyal grace, steadfast mercy, and eternal covenant faithfulness.\n    *   God is never the one who breaks the covenant; His promises remain rock-solid even when His people stumble.\n\n### III. The Heart of True Contrition: Unflinching Confession (vv. 6–7)\n*   **The Plea for Divine Audience:** \"Let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant\" (v. 6a).\n    *   Nehemiah pleads for God’s engaged attention, presenting himself humbly as an *'ebed* [EH-ved], a bondservant with no claim of personal merit.\n*   **The Identification with the Guilty:** \"Confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned\" (v. 6b).\n    *   Like Daniel (Daniel 9) and Ezra (Ezra 9), Nehemiah does not point an accusing finger at others from an ivory tower of self-righteousness.\n    *   He includes himself in the guilt: \"We have sinned... Even I and my father's house.\"\n*   **The Anatomy of Apostasy:** \"We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules\" (v. 7).\n    *   \"Acted very corruptly\" (*chavol chavalnu* [khah-VOLE khah-VAHL-noo])—intensive grammatical construction denoting deep, pervasive, and willful perversion.\n    *   Sin is fundamentally against God: \"against you.\"\n    *   Disobedience was comprehensive: neglecting moral commandments (*mitzvot*), religious statutes (*chuqqim*), and judicial ordinances (*mishpatim*).\n\n### IV. The Ground of Bold Intercession: Pleading God's Word and Promises (vv. 8–10)\n*   **Reminding God of His Word:** \"Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses\" (v. 8a).\n    *   \"Remember\" (*zekhar-na* [zeh-KHOR-nah])—not that God forgets, but calling upon Him to act in alignment with His revealed character and covenant decrees.\n    *   Effective prayer is saturated with Scripture; Nehemiah quotes almost verbatim from Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30.\n*   **The Reality of Divine Chastisement:** \"If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples\" (v. 8b).\n    *   The exile was not bad luck or geopolitical circumstance; it was the direct fulfillment of divine discipline for covenant infidelity (*ma'al* [MAH-al]).\n*   **The Sovereign Promise of Restoration:** \"But if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them... from there I will gather them\" (v. 9).\n    *   *Shuv* [shoov]—genuine repentance, turning around from sin back to God.\n    *   Even if the outcasts are at the furthest horizon (*biqthe ha-shamayim* [biq-TSAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]), God's sovereign arm can reach them, gathering them to the place He chose for His name to dwell (Jerusalem/the temple).\n*   **The Plea of Blood-Bought Ownership:** \"They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand\" (v. 10).\n    *   *Paditha* [pah-DEE-thah]—delivered from bondage, an explicit allusion to the Exodus.\n    *   Nehemiah appeals to God’s past redemptive acts: God cannot abandon the work of His own hands without marring His holy reputation.\n\n### V. The Practical Petition for Providential Favor (v. 11)\n*   **Joining the Fellowship of Worshippers:** \"To the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name\" (v. 11a).\n    *   *Chafetzim le-yir'ah* [khah-fay-TSEEM le-yeer-AW]—godly fear is not craven terror, but a source of supreme joy and holy affection.\n*   **The Specific Request for Providential Success:** \"Give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man\" (v. 11b).\n    *   \"Give success\" (*hatzlichah-na* [hats-lee-KHAH-nah])—prosper the mission by divine favor.\n    *   \"Mercy\" (*rachamim* [rah-khah-MEEM])—compassion, tender favor in the heart of the monarch.\n    *   \"This man\" (*ha'ish hazzeh* [ha-EESH haz-ZEH])—King Artaxerxes, the ruler of the greatest empire on earth, is stripped of his divine pretensions. To Nehemiah, standing before the God of heaven, the Persian emperor is simply \"this man.\"\n*   **The Providential Platform:** \"Now I was cupbearer to the king\" (v. 11c).\n    *   *Mashkeh* [mash-KEH]—an office of extraordinary trust, intimate proximity, and daily access to the emperor.\n    *   God places His people strategically in secular society not for self-indulgence, but for the kingdom of God and the glory of His name.\n\n---\n\n**Pastoral Application:**\n1.  **Examine What Breaks Your Heart:** Are you moved to tears by the spiritual desolation of the church and the reproach brought upon Christ's name, or do you only weep over personal inconveniences and financial losses?\n2.  **Make Prayer Your Primary Weapon, Not a Last Resort:** Before Nehemiah organized a single work crew or spoke to the king, he spent four months on his knees before the God of heaven.\n3.  **Approach God with Holy Reverence:** Avoid flippant, casual prayers. True prayer begins with holy awe before the transcendent, covenant-keeping God.\n4.  **Practice Honest, Corporate Confession:** Never look down upon the failures of the church with smug superiority. Own the sins of God's people and confess: \"We have sinned against You.\"\n5.  **Plead the Promises of Scripture:** Effective prayer does not invent arguments out of human sentiment; it holds God's Word up to Him and says, \"Lord, You have promised.\"\n6.  **Recognize the Transience of Human Power:** Worldly leaders and corporate kings are merely \"men\" in the hands of the Almighty. The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord (Proverbs 21:1).\n7.  **Use Your Providential Platform for God's Kingdom:** Wherever God has placed you—in business, education, government, or homemaking—you are there as a servant of the God of heaven to advance His glory.\n\n**Cross-References:**\n*   **Deuteronomy 30:1–5:** God’s promise to gather His dispersed people from the ends of heaven upon their repentance.\n*   **Daniel 9:3–19:** Daniel’s intercessory prayer of confession and corporate identification for Jerusalem's ruins.\n*   **Ezra 9:5–15:** Ezra’s deep mourning and confession of the guilt of the post-exilic remnant.\n*   **Proverbs 21:1:** \"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will.\"\n*   **Psalm 102:13–17:** The Lord will arise and have pity on Zion when His servants take pleasure in her stones and favor her dust.\n*   **Psalm 137:5–6:** The exiled believer's supreme devotion to Jerusalem above highest earthly joy.\n*   **Hebrews 4:16:** Coming boldly to the throne of grace to find mercy and grace in time of need through our Great High Priest.",

{
  "Content": "# Nehemiah 01, 1-11\n\nOpen your Bibles this morning to the Old Testament book of Nehemiah—Nehemiah chapter 1. \n\nWe are embarking today on a study of one of the most remarkable, instructive, and intensely practical books in all the Old Testament historical narrative. When most Christians think of Nehemiah, their minds immediately race to leadership principles, administrative strategy, and the rebuilding of stone walls. But church, let me tell you at the very outset: if you view Nehemiah primarily as an ancient manual for modern corporate management, you will miss the entire heartbeat of the Holy Spirit in this book. \n\nNehemiah is not first and foremost a book about bricklaying or organizational techniques. It is a book about the glory of God, the sovereign providence of God, the authority of the Word of God, and the indispensable power of God-centered, repentant prayer. \n\nConsider the historical setting for a moment. The year is 445 B.C. The southern kingdom of Judah had fallen to Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians in 586 B.C. because of centuries of relentless, idolatrous rebellion against Yahweh. The glorious temple of Solomon was reduced to ash, the walls of the holy city were leveled, and the people of God were dragged away into captivity. \n\nYet, God had promised through the prophet Jeremiah that after seventy years, the exile would end. And precisely on schedule, God stirred the heart of Cyrus, king of Persia, who had conquered Babylon, to issue a decree in 538 B.C. permitting the Jewish exiles to return to their ancestral homeland. Under Zerubbabel, a remnant returned and rebuilt the altar and eventually completed the second temple around 516 B.C. Decades later, in 458 B.C., Ezra the scribe led a second wave of returnees to re-establish the spiritual, moral, and doctrinal instruction of the Law among the people.\n\nNow, nearly a century has elapsed since that first return under Zerubbabel. And who is Nehemiah? He is not a priest like Ezra. He is not a writing prophet like Zechariah or Malachi. He is a Jewish layman living in exile, serving in the highest corridors of Persian imperial power. Yet here we see what happens when the sovereign God takes hold of a layman whose heart is completely captive to the honor of God's name.\n\nFollow along as I read the first chapter of Nehemiah—verses 1 through 11, from the English Standard Version:\n\n\u003e **\"The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel, that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem. And they said to me, 'The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire.'**\n\u003e\n\u003e **As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven. And I said, 'O Lord God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned. We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses. Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, \"If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.\" They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand. O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.'**\n\u003e\n\u003e **Now I was cupbearer to the king.\"**\n\nChurch, the big idea of this passage is unmistakable: **When God’s work lies in ruin and His name is brought into reproach, true spiritual leadership begins not with human schemes, but with a broken heart that seeks the sovereign, covenant-keeping God in repentant, promise-claiming prayer.**\n\nNotice how the narrative unfolds in five distinct movements.\n\n---\n\n### I. The Ruin of the Remnant and the Broken Heart of the Leader (vv. 1–4)\n\nLook at verse 1: **\"The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel...\"**\n\nNehemiah dates his memoirs with historical precision. The month of Chislev corresponds to our late November and December. The \"twentieth year\" refers to the twentieth regnal year of Artaxerxes I Longimanus, which places this firmly in late autumn of 445 B.C. \n\nWhere is Nehemiah? He is in \"Susa the citadel\" (*Shushan habbirah*). Susa was located about 150 miles north of the Persian Gulf, in modern-day southwest Iran. It was the lavish, fortified winter residence of the Persian monarchs. It was a fortress of imperial luxury, guarded by the legendary Persian Immortals, surrounded by manicured gardens, magnificent colonnades, and every indulgence the ancient world could offer.\n\nNehemiah had every earthly reason to be comfortable. He had achieved what very few exiles ever achieved: status, safety, wealth, and proximity to the most powerful monarch on the globe. He was insulated from the dust, poverty, and struggles of Judea, which lay nearly a thousand miles to the west—a dangerous, four-month journey away.\n\nYet look at verse 2: **\"that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.\"**\n\nHanani, his biological brother (as Nehemiah 7:2 confirms), arrives from the homeland with a delegation. Notice Nehemiah’s priority. He doesn't ask about Persian politics, business opportunities, or foreign gossip. His first question is about the people of God and the city of God: \"How is the remnant? How is Jerusalem?\"\n\nFolks, here is the first mark of a true man of God: *His heart is tethered to the condition of God’s people.* You can tell what a man loves by what he inquires about. Nehemiah’s physical address was the palace in Susa, but his spiritual home was Jerusalem.\n\nAnd what was the news? Verse 3 delivers the crushing blow: **\"And they said to me, 'The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire.'\"**\n\nThis report is devastating. The word for \"remnant\" (*hannish'arim* [han-nish-ah-REEM]) refers to the small, fragile band of Jews who had returned to the province of Yehud. And how are they described? They are in \"great trouble\" (*ra'ah gedolah* [rah-AW geh-do-LAW])—in acute affliction, poverty, vulnerability, and misery. \n\nWorse still, they are in \"shame\" or \"reproach\" (*cherpah* [kher-PAW]). In the ancient Near East, a city without walls was an invitation to slaughter and mockery. Surrounding pagan enemies—the Samaritans, the Ammonites, the Arabs—harassed the people, raided their crops, and ridiculed their faith. \n\nYou see, church, the real issue was not merely the civic inconvenience of tumbled stones. The real issue was the glory of Yahweh! When the holy city of God was a pile of charred rubble and His covenant people were defenseless and humiliated, the pagan world looked upon them and concluded: *Their God is weak. Their God has failed.* God's holy name was being blasphemed among the nations.\n\nNow look at Nehemiah's reaction in verse 4. This is our anchor point: **\"As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.\"**\n\nNotice what Nehemiah did *not* do. He did not immediately call a committee. He did not draft a fifteen-point strategic reconstruction plan. He did not draft a petition to the emperor. He did not erupt in anger against the governors in Judah for their incompetence. \n\nHe collapsed. He sat down. The news hit him like a physical blow. He wept, and he mourned for days (*ebkeh va-et'abbalah* [ev-KEH va-et-ahb-bah-LAW]). He afflicted his soul with fasting and poured out his heart in relentless prayer. \n\nChurch, let me ask you a piercing question: *What makes you weep?* \n\nDoes your soul ever ache over the spiritual desolation of the church? When you see false doctrine rampant, when you see pulpits surrendered to entertainment, when you see professing Christians living like pagans, when you see the gospel compromised and the name of Jesus Christ dragged through the mud of cultural reproach—does it break you? \n\nOr do you only weep over your personal finances, your broken health, or your damaged pride? John Knox famously cried out, \"Give me Scotland, or I die!\" The Apostle Paul wrote in Romans 9:2 that he had \"great sorrow and unceasing anguish\" in his heart for his countrymen. Nehemiah wept because the ruin of Jerusalem was a reproach upon the glory of God.\n\nAnd notice to whom he turned: \"before the God of heaven\" (*lipne Elohei ha-shamayim* [lip-NAY el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]). Not to the king of Persia. Not to human counselors. But to the Sovereign of the universe. \n\nAnd take note of the calendar, folks. This prayer begins in the month of Chislev (December). He does not speak to King Artaxerxes until the month of Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1), which is April! That is four solid months of weeping, fasting, and interceding in secret before he ever takes one single public step. Spiritual leaders do their primary work on their knees before they ever stand on their feet.\n\n---\n\n### II. The God-Centered Approach to Prayer: Adoration and Reverence (v. 5)\n\nNow, in verses 5 through 11, the Holy Spirit preserves for us the anatomy of Nehemiah's prayer. It is a masterpiece of biblical intercession, standing alongside the prayers of Daniel in Daniel 9 and Ezra in Ezra 9. \n\nLook at how he begins in verse 5: **\"And I said, 'O Lord God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments...'\"**\n\nNotice the order. Nehemiah does not barge into the throne room of the Almighty with a laundry list of demands. He begins with *adoration*. He begins with the character of God. \n\nHe addresses Him first by His covenant name: *Yahweh*—the self-existent, eternal, I AM THAT I AM, the God who reveals Himself in covenant relationship to His people. Then he calls Him *Elohei ha-shamayim*—\"God of heaven.\" Why? Because Nehemiah is standing in Susa, where the Persian king was hailed as the \"King of Kings\" and the master of the earth. But Nehemiah looks past the imperial throne of Persia to the One whose throne is in the heavens, who does whatever He pleases (Psalm 115:3). \n\nHe calls Him \"the great and awesome God\" (*El haggadol ve-hannora* [ALE hag-gah-DOLE ve-han-no-RAW]). The word *nora* comes from the root *yare* [yah-RAY], meaning \"to fear\" or \"to revere.\" God is not our \"pal.\" He is not our buddy upstairs. He is the terrifyingly holy, infinitely transcendent, all-powerful Sovereign before whom the seraphim cover their faces! \n\nChurch, so much modern evangelical praying is shallow, irreverent, and flippant. People approach the holy God as if He were an Amazon delivery service, demanding that He fulfill their petty desires. Biblical prayer begins in the dust, trembling before the majesty and holiness of the Almighty.\n\nYet, God is not only transcendent; He is also near and faithful. Look at the second half of verse 5: \"...who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments.\" \n\nThe Hebrew word here is *chesed* [KHEH-sed]. It is one of the richest words in the entire Old Testament. It speaks of God’s loyal love, His unfailing, covenant-keeping mercy. God does not break His word. If there is a breakdown in the covenant relationship, it is never on God's side. God is always faithful. Nehemiah anchors his soul not in the shifting circumstances of Jerusalem, but in the immutable character and covenant faithfulness of God.\n\n---\n\n### III. The Heart of True Contrition: Unflinching Confession (vv. 6–7)\n\nOnce you see the holiness and faithfulness of God, you are instantly confronted with your own sinfulness. And that leads directly to confession.\n\nLook at verse 6: **\"let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.\"**\n\nNehemiah pleads for divine audience. He asks God to bend His ear and open His eyes to the plight of His people. He prays \"day and night\"—this was not a hurried two-minute devotion before running off to work; it was sustained, agonized intercession.\n\nAnd what does he do? He confesses sin. But look carefully at *how* he confesses. Does Nehemiah say, \"Lord, those wicked people back in Judah have really blown it\"? Does he say, \"Lord, look at those miserable compromises made by the priests in Jerusalem\"? \n\nNo! He says: \"confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which *we* have sinned against you. Even *I and my father's house* have sinned.\"\n\nThis is staggering. Nehemiah was a godly man. He was living an upright, faithful life in the midst of a pagan empire. Yet he does not separate himself from the guilty community. He does not point an accusing finger from an ivory tower of moral superiority. He kneels in the dirt alongside the worst offenders and cries out, \"We have sinned! I have sinned!\"\n\nListen to me, congregation: You will never be an effective intercessor for the people of God until you stop condemning them with self-righteous arrogance and start identifying with them in broken confession. It is easy to criticize the state of the church. It is easy to sit behind a keyboard and dissect the spiritual failures of our generation. It is entirely another thing to weep, fast, and say, \"Lord, we are guilty. I am part of this compromised generation. Forgive us!\"\n\nAnd notice how specific and unsparing his confession is in verse 7: **\"We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.\"**\n\nThe Hebrew grammar here is profound. \"We have acted very corruptly\" is *chavol chavalnu* [khah-VOLE khah-VAHL-noo]. It is an infinitive absolute combined with a finite verb—literally, \"in corrupting, we have corrupted ourselves.\" It is an intensive, emphatic Hebrew idiom. Nehemiah is saying, \"Lord, we haven't merely made minor mistakes; we have perverted our ways to the uttermost! We are thoroughly, ruinously guilty!\"\n\nAnd notice the nature of sin: \"against *you*.\" Just like David in Psalm 51:4 (\"Against you, you only, have I sinned\"), Nehemiah recognizes that all sin is ultimately cosmic treason against a holy God. We have disregarded His moral commandments (*mitzvot*), His ceremonial statutes (*chuqqim*), and His judicial rules (*mishpatim*). Israel had no excuse. They possessed the divine revelation given to Moses, and they trampled it underfoot.\n\n---\n\n### IV. The Ground of Bold Intercession: Pleading God's Word and Promises (vv. 8–10)\n\nHaving confessed the sin, how does Nehemiah dare to ask for restoration? On what basis can a guilty people ask for mercy? Look at verse 8: **\"Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses...\"**\n\n\"Remember\" (*zekhar-na* [zeh-KHOR-nah]). Does God suffer from amnesia? Does the omniscient Lord forget His promises? Of course not. In biblical Hebrew, when God \"remembers,\" it means He acts decisively in accordance with His covenant obligations (as in Genesis 8:1, when God \"remembered Noah\"). \n\nNehemiah is doing what every great saint of God has always done: *He is praying Scripture back to God.* \n\nLook at the quotation in verses 8 and 9: **\"saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'\"**\n\nNehemiah is quoting almost verbatim from Deuteronomy chapter 4, Deuteronomy 28 through 30, and Leviticus 26. \n\nFirst, he acknowledges the justice of God’s judgment: \"If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you.\" The Hebrew word for unfaithful is *ma'al* [MAH-al], which speaks of covenant betrayal. Nehemiah admits that the Babylonian exile was not a tragedy of bad foreign policy; it was the holy judgment of God! God had kept His threat.\n\nBut then he lays hold of the promise of grace: \"but if you return to me...\" The word for return is *shuv* [shoov]—the classic Hebrew term for repentance. It means an about-face, turning away from sin and returning in heart and obedience to Yahweh. \n\nAnd what did God promise? God promised that even if His outcasts were scattered to the furthest corners under heaven (*biqthe ha-shamayim* [biq-TSAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]), He would sovereignly gather them and bring them back to \"the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there\"—which is Jerusalem!\n\nFolks, do you see the brilliance and power of this prayer? Nehemiah holds the Word of God up before the face of God and says: \"Lord, You kept the first part of Your Word—You scattered us when we rebelled. Now, Lord, keep the second part of Your Word! We are turning to You. Gather us! Rebuild the place where Your name dwells!\"\n\nThe most powerful prayers you can ever utter are the prayers that simply say, \"Lord, You have spoken. You have promised. For the sake of Your own integrity, fulfill Your Word!\"\n\nAnd then look at verse 10: **\"They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.\"**\n\nNehemiah appeals to God’s past redemption. \"Redeemed\" (*paditha* [pah-DEE-thah]) points directly back to the Exodus, where God shattered Pharaoh’s grip with His strong hand. Nehemiah is saying, \"Lord, these people belong to You. You bought them with blood and power. You cannot abandon the work of Your own hands, lest the pagan nations say that Yahweh was unable to protect His own people!\"\n\n---\n\n### V. The Practical Petition for Providential Favor (v. 11)\n\nFinally, after four months of adoration, confession, and pleading God’s promises, Nehemiah comes to his specific, practical petition. \n\nLook at verse 11: **\"O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.\"**\n\nNotice how he describes true believers: they \"delight to fear your name\" (*chafetzim le-yir'ah et-shimcha* [khah-fay-TSEEM le-yeer-AW et shim-KHAW]). What a magnificent phrase! Godly fear is not a cowering dread of a cruel tyrant; it is a holy delight, an affectionate reverence for the majestic name and honor of God. Nehemiah knows he is not alone; there is a faithful remnant whose greatest joy is the fear of the Lord.\n\nAnd then comes the petition: \"give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of *this man*.\"\n\nNotice that phrase: \"this man\" (*ha'ish hazzeh* [ha-EESH haz-ZEH]). Who is he talking about? He is talking about Artaxerxes, the Great King of Persia, the ruler of an empire that stretched from India to Ethiopia! To the ancient world, Artaxerxes was virtually a god. His word was absolute law; with a flick of his wrist, he could execute thousands.\n\nYet, to Nehemiah, who had just spent four months staring into the blinding majesty of the God of heaven, the Persian monarch is reduced to his true size: *he is merely \"this man.\"* He is made of dust. His breath is in his nostrils. His heart is like a stream of water in the sovereign hand of Yahweh; He turns it wherever He wills (Proverbs 21:1). \n\nWhen you spend time on your face before the King of kings, earthly rulers lose their power to intimidate you.\n\nAnd why did he need mercy from the king? The chapter concludes with a simple, striking autobiographical statement: **\"Now I was cupbearer to the king.\"**\n\nThe cupbearer (*mashkeh* [mash-KEH]) was not a mere butler. In the Persian court, the cupbearer was one of the most high-ranking, influential officers in the entire empire. Because assassination by poison was a constant threat, the cupbearer was responsible for selecting, guarding, and tasting the royal wine and food before the king touched it. \n\nTo hold this position, a man had to possess unimpeachable integrity, unswerving loyalty, and deep wisdom. He had daily, intimate, confidential access to the monarch. He was a trusted royal counselor.\n\nDo you see the providence of God, church? Decades before this crisis ever erupted, the sovereign God of heaven was moving His invisible chess pieces on the board of history. God took an exiled Jewish boy named Nehemiah and elevated him through the ranks of the Persian civil service until he was standing right beside the emperor's elbow! \n\nGod had placed Nehemiah in the palace for such a time as this. But Nehemiah didn't view his high office as a means for personal wealth, career advancement, or self-aggrandizement. He saw it as a providential platform to be risked for the kingdom of God and the restoration of God’s people.\n\n---\n\n### Conclusion and Appeal\n\nAs we close this morning, let these truths settle deep into your soul. \n\nWhen you look out at the landscape of the church today, do you see walls broken down? Do you see the gates burned with fire? Do you see moral compromise, biblical illiteracy, and cultural reproach resting upon the church of Jesus Christ? \n\nIf you do, what is your response? \n\nWill you merely complain? Will you throw up your hands in cynical despair? Or will you, like Nehemiah, fall on your knees before the God of heaven? Will you weep? Will you fast? Will you confess the sins of our generation, identifying yourself with the failure of God's people? Will you open the Word of God and plead His promises back to Him?\n\nAnd remember, church: Nehemiah points us ultimately to a far greater Servant. \n\nNehemiah left the palace of Susa to visit the rubble of Jerusalem. But our Lord Jesus Christ left the eternal ivory palaces of heaven and stepped into the broken, sin-cursed rubble of this fallen world. \n\nNehemiah sat and wept over the ruin of Jerusalem. But Jesus Christ stood on the Mount of Olives and wept bitter tears over Jerusalem's spiritual blindness. \n\nNehemiah confessed the sins of a people he loved, though he was not individually responsible for the exile. But Jesus Christ took the sins of His people upon His own sinless shoulders! He who knew no sin became sin for us on the cross, drinking the cup of God's wrath to the very dregs, so that the broken walls of our ruined lives might be completely rebuilt, and that we might be reconciled to the God of heaven forever.\n\nIf you are outside of Christ today, your soul is a city without walls, exposed to the wrath of a holy God. I urge you: do not delay. Turn from your sin in repentance (*shuv*), cast yourself upon the covenant steadfast love (*chesed*) of God, and find eternal refuge in Jesus Christ, the Builder and Redeemer of His people.\n\nLet us pray.\n\n*O Lord God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love: forgive us for our shallow prayers, our dry eyes, and our cold hearts. Break our hearts for what breaks Yours. Awaken in our souls a relentless passion for the glory of Your name and the purity of Your church. Teach us to pray Your promises with boldness and faith, and use our lives—in whatever station You have placed us—for the advancement of Your eternal kingdom. We ask it in the exalted, sovereign name of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior. Amen.*",

{
  "Content": "# A Heart Broken for God's Glory\n\n### Scripture: Nehemiah 1:1–11\n\nThe book of Nehemiah is frequently treated as an ancient treatise on leadership, organizational strategy, and civic administration. Yet to reduce this narrative to principles of human management is to miss its theological heartbeat. Nehemiah is not fundamentally a book about bricklaying or administrative technique; it is a profound historical testimony to divine sovereignty, covenant fidelity, the authority of Scripture, and the essential priority of God-centered, repentant prayer.\n\nThe historical setting opens in 445 B.C., roughly a century after the initial return of the Jewish exiles under Zerubbabel (538 B.C.) and thirteen years after Ezra’s arrival in Jerusalem (458 B.C.). The temple had been rebuilt, and the Law had been reinstated, but Jerusalem remained vulnerable, demoralized, and culturally disgraced. It was into this critical juncture that God raised up Nehemiah—not a priest or a writing prophet, but a godly layman occupying an office of extraordinary influence within the Persian royal court.\n\n#### The Desolation of Jerusalem and the Brokenness of the Leader (vv. 1–4)\n\nNehemiah dates his memoir with historical precision: the month of Chislev (November–December) in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I Longimanus (v. 1). He resided in \"Susa the citadel\" (*Shushan habbirah*), the lavish, fortified winter capital of the Persian Empire. Surrounded by imperial luxury, security, and prestige, Nehemiah enjoyed every earthly incentive to remain complacent and detached from the plight of his ancestral homeland a thousand miles away.\n\nYet when his brother Hanani arrived with a delegation from Judah (v. 2), Nehemiah’s immediate concern was neither personal advancement nor court politics. He inquired \"concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.\" His spiritual affections were anchored to the condition of God’s covenant people.\n\nHanani’s report was devastating (v. 3): the surviving remnant (*hannish'arim* [han-nish-ah-REEM]) was in \"great trouble\" (*ra'ah gedolah* [rah-AW geh-do-LAW]) and \"shame\" or \"reproach\" (*cherpah* [kher-PAW]). The walls lay in breaches (*meforetzet* [meh-fo-REH-tset]), and the wooden gates were charred ruins (*yatzetu va'esh* [yaht-seh-TOO vah-ESH]). In the ancient Near East, a defenseless city invited continuous raids, oppression, and ridicule from hostile neighbors. Far more critically, the destitution of Jerusalem was a reproach upon the name of Yahweh. The surrounding nations looked upon the broken rubble and concluded that Israel’s God was impotent or indifferent.\n\nNehemiah's reaction reveals the heart of true spiritual leadership (v. 4): \"As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.\" He did not hastily launch an activist campaign, organize a committee, or petition the king. He collapsed under the weight of godly grief. For four months—from Chislev to Nisan—he mourned, fasted, and laid the crisis before \"the God of heaven\" (*Elohei ha-shamayim* [el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim]). Spiritual victories are won in the secret place of prayer long before any public action is undertaken.\n\n#### The God-Centered Approach: Adoration and Reverence (v. 5)\n\nVerses 5 through 11 provide an inspired model of biblical intercession. Nehemiah begins not with his personal distress or a litany of requests, but with reverent adoration of the sovereign God:\n\n\u003e \"O Lord God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments...\" (v. 5)\n\nNehemiah invokes the sacred covenant name *Yahweh*, joined with the transcendent title \"God of heaven.\" Living in the shadow of an earthly emperor who claimed cosmic dominion, Nehemiah looked beyond the throne of Persia to the One who rules supreme over the universe. He describes Him as \"the great and awesome God\" (*El haggadol ve-hannora* [ALE hag-gah-DOLE ve-han-no-RAW]). The term *nora* conveys holy dread and majesty. Effective prayer does not approach God with flippant familiarity; it trembles before divine holiness.\n\nSimultaneously, Nehemiah grounds his hope in God’s covenant fidelity. Yahweh is the God who guards His covenant and preserves His *chesed* [KHEH-sed]—His loyal, unfailing, steadfast covenant love. Though human fidelity wavers, divine faithfulness remains immutable.\n\n#### The Heart of True Contrition: Unflinching Confession (vv. 6–7)\n\nTrue adoration inevitably exposes human sinfulness. Pleading for God’s ear to be attentive and His eyes open (v. 6), Nehemiah confesses the sins of Israel with remarkable corporate solidarity: \"confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.\"\n\nLike Daniel (Dan. 9) and Ezra (Ezra 9), Nehemiah refuses to adopt an attitude of superior detachment. Though living an exemplary life, he does not isolate himself from the guilty community. He includes himself in the confession: *we* have sinned; *I* have sinned. \n\nHis confession is unsparing and precise (v. 7): \"We have acted very corruptly against you.\" The Hebrew construction *chavol chavalnu* [khah-VOLE khah-VAHL-noo] uses an intensive infinitive absolute, literally denoting \"in corrupting, we have utterly corrupted ourselves.\" Sin is acknowledged in its true theological horror as cosmic treason against God Himself (\"against you\"), evidenced by the deliberate abandonment of His moral commandments (*mitzvot*), ceremonial statutes (*chuqqim*), and judicial ordinances (*mishpatim*).\n\n#### The Ground of Intercession: Pleading God's Promises (vv. 8–10)\n\nHaving acknowledged the justice of God’s wrath, Nehemiah appeals boldly to the revealed Word of God: \"Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses\" (v. 8). In biblical usage, divine remembering (*zekhar-na* [zeh-KHOR-nah]) denotes decisive action in accordance with covenant promises. \n\nNehemiah quotes the warnings and promises of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30. He acknowledges that the dispersion of Israel was the exact fulfillment of divine judgment for covenant infidelity (*ma'al* [MAH-al]). Yet he simultaneously lays hold of the promised mercy: if the people return (*shuv* [shoov]—repent) to Yahweh, God will gather them from the uttermost parts of heaven and restore them to the place chosen for His name to dwell (v. 9).\n\nNehemiah's intercession is thoroughly Word-saturated. He prays God’s own promises back to Him. He further appeals to God’s redemptive ownership (v. 10): \"They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed (*paditha* [pah-DEE-thah]) by your great power and by your strong hand.\" Recalling the Exodus, Nehemiah reminds the Lord that His own glory and redemptive reputation are at stake among the nations.\n\n#### The Practical Petition and Sovereign Providence (v. 11)\n\nOnly after four months of adoration, corporate repentance, and scriptural pleading does Nehemiah bring his specific petition:\n\n\u003e \"O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.\" (v. 11)\n\nNehemiah identifies with the faithful remnant whose supreme joy is to \"delight to fear your name\" (*chafetzim le-yir'ah et-shimcha* [khah-fay-TSEEM le-yeer-AW et shim-KHAW]). True fear of God is not paralyzing terror, but a joyful, affectionate reverence.\n\nHe asks for providential success (*hatzlichah-na* [hats-lee-KHAH-nah]) and mercy (*rachamim* [rah-khah-MEEM]) before \"this man\" (*ha'ish hazzeh* [ha-EESH haz-ZEH]). To the ancient world, Artaxerxes was an omnipotent, god-like potentate whose word meant life or death. Spiritual leadership looks directly at the full severity of ruins without flinching or sugarcoating.\n*   **Prudent Discretion (v. 16):**\n    *   The civic magistrates, priests, and nobles knew nothing yet. Spiritual wisdom discerns the timing between silent contemplation and public mobilization.\n\n### IV. Mobilizing the Remnant for Holy Work (vv. 17–18)\n*   **Confronting the Reality of Reproach (v. 17a):**\n    *   \"You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned.\"\n    *   Nehemiah does not indulge in flattery or psychological pep-talks; he confronts the leaders with the stark truth of their misery.\n*   **The Call to Vindicate God's Name (v. 17b):**\n    *   \"Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision\" (*cherpah* [kher-PAW]—reproach, shame).\n    *   The motive is not civic pride or personal legacy, but removing the pagan mockery from the holy city and vindicating the glory of Yahweh.\n*   **The Testimony of Sovereign Power (v. 18a):**\n    *   \"And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me.\"\n    *   Spiritual motivation flows from recounting what God has done.\n*   **The Resolute Response of the Remnant (v. 18b):**\n    *   \"And they said, 'Let us rise up and build' (*naqum uvaninu* [nah-QOOM oo-vah-NEE-noo]).\"\n    *   \"So they strengthened their hands for the good work\" (*vaychazzequ yedeihem lattovah* [vay-khaz-zeh-QOO yeh-day-HEM lat-to-VAH]).\n\n### V. Defiant Faith Against Worldly Intimidation (vv. 19–20)\n*   **The Alliance of Mockery and Slander (v. 19):**\n    *   Joined by Geshem the Arab—surrounding Israel from the north (Samaria), east (Ammon), and south (Arabia).\n    *   *The Tactics of the Adversary:* Jeering (*vayyal'igu* [vay-yal-EE-goo]), despising (*vayyivzu* [vay-yiv-ZOO]), and slandering with charges of sedition: \"Are you rebelling against the king?\"\n*   **The Theological Triad of Victory (v. 20a):**\n    *   Nehemiah does not produce Artaxerxes' letters or argue legalities with the pagans.\n    *   *The Ultimate Authority:* \"The God of heaven will make us prosper\" (*Elohei ha-shamayim hu yatzliach lanu* [el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim HOO yats-LEE-akh LAH-noo]).\n    *   *The Sacred Calling:* \"And we his servants will arise and build.\"\n*   **The Wall of Demarcation (v. 20b):**\n    *   \"But you have no portion or right or claim [memorial] in Jerusalem\" (*cheleq u-tsedaqah ve-zikkaron* [KHEH-leq oo-tsed-ah-QAH veh-zik-kah-RONE]).\n    *   A bold declaration of ecclesiastical separation. The enemies of God have no share in the covenant inheritance, no legal standing in the kingdom, and no memorial among the redeemed.\n\n---\n\n**Pastoral Application:**\n1.  **When Gripped by Fear, Fire an Arrow Prayer to Heaven:** Even when terror strikes suddenly, months of private devotion will erupt into spontaneous, effective reliance upon God.\n2.  **Rest in the Sovereign Hand of God Over Human Hearts:** Earthly rulers, employers, and authorities are entirely under the sovereign sway of the Almighty (Proverbs 21:1).\n3.  **Marry Fervent Prayer with Methodical Preparation:** Nehemiah prayed for four months, but he also calculated travel times, estimated timber requirements, and devised an administrative strategy.\n4.  **Inspect the Ruins Honestly Before Undertaking Reformation:** True spiritual reformation requires that we look directly at doctrinal compromise and moral failure without minimizing the cost.\n5.  **Cast a Vision Centered on God's Glory, Not Human Ambition:** The removal of *cherpah* (reproach) from God’s name is the only worthy motivation for spiritual labors.\n6.  **Expect Demonic Opposition Whenever the Church Advances:** If the world is pleased with your ministry, you are not seeking the true welfare of God’s people.\n7.  **Maintain Strict Separation from Worldly Partnerships:** The church must never compromise with pagan methods or seek alliances with those who have no portion in Christ.\n\n**Cross-References:**\n*   **Proverbs 21:1:** \"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will.\"\n*   **Ezra 4:21 \u0026 Ezra 7:28:** Artaxerxes’ previous prohibition contrasted with God’s hand strengthening His servant.\n*   **Psalm 118:6:** \"The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?\"\n*   **Luke 14:28–30:** Counting the cost of construction before laying the foundation.\n*   **2 Corinthians 6:14–17:** The holy demarcation between the temple of God and idols.\n*   **Matthew 16:18:** Christ’s sovereign promise that the gates of hell shall not prevail against His church.",

{
  "Content": "# Nehemiah 02, 1-20\n\nOpen your Bibles this morning to Nehemiah chapter 2. Today we come to the second chapter of this magnificent historical narrative, and we see the direct, dramatic answer to the prayers that were offered in chapter 1.\n\nIf you were with us for our study of chapter 1, you will remember that Nehemiah, though living in the lap of luxury and security in the Persian winter capital of Susa, was shattered by the news brought by his brother Hanani. The remnant in Judea was in \"great trouble and shame,\" the walls of Jerusalem were broken down, and the gates were charred rubble. And what did Nehemiah do? He did not jump into immediate political activism. He sat down, wept, mourned, fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven.\n\nNow, between the end of chapter 1 and the beginning of chapter 2, four long months have passed. Nehemiah first heard the devastating report in the month of Chislev—our November or December. The opening verse of chapter 2 begins in the month of Nisan—our March or April. \n\nFor one hundred and twenty days, Nehemiah waited on God. For four months, he poured out his heart in secret intercession. But true prayer is never an excuse for inaction. Prayer is the indispensable preparation for action. And in chapter 2, the sovereign God of heaven swings open the iron doors of Persian imperial power and moves His servant from the privacy of the prayer closet directly onto the stage of world history.\n\nFollow along as I read Nehemiah chapter 2, verses 1 through 20, from the English Standard Version:\n\n\u003e **\"In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence. And the king said to me, 'Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart.' Then I was very much afraid. I said to the king, 'Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?'**\n\u003e\n\u003e **Then the king said to me, 'What are you requesting?' So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king, 'If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it.' And the king said to me (the queen sitting next to him), 'How long will your journey be, and when will you return?' So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **And I said to the king, 'If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah, and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy.' And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen. But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days. Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode. I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire. Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no place for the animal that was under me to pass. Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned. And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **Then I said to them, 'You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision.' And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, 'Let us rise up and build.' So they strengthened their hands for the good work.**\n\u003e\n\u003e **But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, 'What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?' Then I replied to them, 'The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem.'\"**\n\nChurch, the great doctrinal truth running through this entire chapter is this: **The sovereign God advances His redemptive work and overcomes hostile opposition by placing His good hand upon praying, courageous servants who plan with wisdom and rally His people for His glory.**\n\nNotice the five strategic movements in this text.\n\n---\n\n### I. Sovereign Favor in the Imperial Palace (vv. 1–8)\n\nLook at verse 1: **\"In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence.\"**\n\nHere is Nehemiah, performing his regular duties as royal cupbearer. But something is different today. For four months he had managed to conceal his inner heartbreak behind a professional demeanor. But you can only carry an agonizing spiritual burden for so long before it begins to leak through the facade.\n\nLook at verse 2: **\"And the king said to me, 'Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart.' Then I was very much afraid.\"**\n\nNow, why was Nehemiah \"very much afraid\" (*va'ira me'od me'od* [vah-ee-RAH meh-ODE meh-ODE])? In our culture, sadness draws sympathy. In the ancient Persian court, sadness drew execution! \n\nTo show a dejected face before the Persian monarch was a capital crime. It implied that the king’s presence was not a source of absolute joy, or worse, that you were plotting treason or harboring discontent with his reign. Esther herself risked death simply by approaching the king uninvited (Esther 4:11). \n\nFurthermore, Artaxerxes was the very king who, years earlier, had received a slanderous letter from the enemies of the Jews and had officially decreed that the rebuilding of Jerusalem be stopped by royal command (Ezra 4:17–22)! Nehemiah was about to ask this despotic ruler to reverse his own imperial foreign policy. One misstep, one perceived insult, and Nehemiah’s head would roll across the polished marble floor.\n\nYet notice his response in verse 3: **\"I said to the king, 'Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?'\"**\n\nNehemiah combines supreme respect with unflinching honesty. He uses the standard court etiquette (\"Let the king live forever!\"), but he does not deny his sorrow. And notice his wisdom: he does not use the politically loaded word \"Jerusalem.\" He appeals to a universal ancient Near Eastern value that even a pagan monarch revered—honor for \"the place of my fathers' graves.\"\n\nThen comes the pivotal moment in verse 4: **\"Then the king said to me, 'What are you requesting?' So I prayed to the God of heaven.\"**\n\nFolks, look at that phrase: *\"So I prayed to the God of heaven.\"* \n\nThe king is sitting right in front of him, staring at him, waiting for an immediate answer. Nehemiah cannot drop to his knees. He cannot close his eyes. He cannot audibly recite Psalm 23. This is what theologians call an \"arrow prayer\"—a silent, instantaneous flash of the soul directed to the throne of grace! \n\nBetween the king’s question and Nehemiah’s answer, a telegram was delivered to heaven: *Lord, help me right now!*\n\nChurch, hear me on this: you cannot pray spontaneous arrow prayers with power unless you have spent four months in the prayer closet! The reason Nehemiah could pray on his feet in a single second was because he had been living on his knees for one hundred and twenty days. If your prayer life consists only of emergency flare-prayers when a crisis hits, you are spiritually bankrupt. Spontaneous prayer must be the overflow of habitual, disciplined communion with God.\n\nFortified by that split-second prayer, Nehemiah makes his bold request in verse 5: **\"If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it.\"**\n\nLook at verse 6: **\"And the king said to me (the queen sitting next to him), 'How long will your journey be, and when will you return?' So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time.\"**\n\nThe parenthetical detail—\"the queen sitting next to him\"—is fascinating. Historians identify her as Queen Damaspia. The fact that the queen was present indicates this was an intimate, private dinner, not a raucous state banquet. God orchestrated the exact setting! Artaxerxes doesn't ask, \"Why should I reverse my policy?\" He asks, \"How long will you be gone, and when will you come back?\" The king valued Nehemiah so highly that his primary concern was losing his trusted cupbearer.\n\nAnd look at Nehemiah's preparation in verses 7 and 8. He didn't just pray; he planned! \n\nHe asks for royal letters of safe passage to the governors of the province Beyond the River (*'Ever-ha-Nahar* [EH-ver ha-nah-HAR]—the territory west of the Euphrates). Then he asks for a timber requisition letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's royal park (*pardes* [par-DAYS]), for cedar beams to rebuild the fortress of the temple, the city wall, and his own residence. Nehemiah had calculated travel times, logistics, and material costs during those four months of prayer.\n\nAnd what happened? Verse 8 gives us the divine explanation: **\"And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.\"**\n\nThe Hebrew is magnificent: *kiyad-Elohay hatovah 'alay* [kee-yad el-o-HAI ha-to-VAH ah-LAI]. \n\nNehemiah does not say, \"The king granted it because I am a brilliant negotiator.\" He does not say, \"The king granted it because Artaxerxes was having a generous day.\" He points directly to the sovereign providence of the Almighty! \n\nRemember Proverbs 21:1: \"The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will.\" The most powerful monarch in the world was putty in the hands of the God of heaven. When the \"good hand of God\" is upon you, earthly rulers become instruments of divine grace.\n\n---\n\n### II. The Gathering Clouds of Demonic Hostility (vv. 9–10)\n\nIn verse 9, Nehemiah arrives in the trans-Euphrates province armed with royal letters and escorted by Persian army officers and cavalry. But look at verse 10:\n\n**\"But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.\"**\n\nChurch, write this down in your spiritual memory: *The moment you set your heart to seek the welfare of God's people and the glory of God's name, the enemy will mobilize his forces against you.*\n\nWho are these men? \nSanballat the Horonite was the governor of Samaria, reigning to the north of Judah. He was an influential, ruthless pagan politician. \nTobiah was an Ammonite official who held sway east of the Jordan. \n\nNotice how the text describes their reaction: \"it displeased them greatly.\" In the Hebrew, it is an emphatic idiom: *vayyera lahem ra'ah gedolah* [vay-YEH-rah lah-HEM rah-AW geh-do-LAW]—literally, \"it was evil to them with a great evil.\" It infuriated them to the core. Why? Because \"someone had come to seek the welfare (*tovah* [to-VAH]) of the people of Israel.\"\n\nThe world doesn't mind a weak, compromised, defenseless church. The world is perfectly content when the people of God are living in reproach, conforming to the culture, and keeping their heads down. But the minute a servant of God arrives with spiritual backbone, determined to rebuild the broken walls of truth and righteousness, hell erupts in fury! Do not be surprised by opposition. If you never encounter the devil walking down the street, it's because you're walking in the same direction!\n\n---\n\n### III. Realistic Assessment in Secret (vv. 11–16)\n\nNehemiah arrives in Jerusalem in verse 11, and he waits three days. \n\nWhy three days? He needed rest after a grueling, three-month journey. But more importantly, he needed time to be still before God. He avoided the trap of modern leadership: rushing into town, calling a press conference, and announcing grand schemes before understanding the facts.\n\nThen look at verses 12 and 13: **\"Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem... I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire.\"**\n\nUnder the cover of darkness, Nehemiah rides out on a single mount to inspect the devastation. \n\nNotice the word \"inspected\" (*shover* [sho-VAYR]) in verses 13 and 15. In biblical Hebrew, *shavar* is a diagnostic medical term. It was used of a physician probing a fractured bone or inspecting a deep wound to determine the exact nature of the injury. It was also used of an architect examining the structural integrity of a foundation. \n\nNehemiah did not rely on hearsay. He did not engage in wishful thinking. He went out into the dead of night, smelling the charred wood, looking at the cracked stones, measuring the breaches. \n\nLook at verse 14: **\"Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no place for the animal that was under me to pass.\"** \n\nThe rubble was so immense, the destruction so complete, that his donkey could not even find footing to squeeze through the debris! Nehemiah stared straight into the horrifying reality of the ruin.\n\nCongregation, true spiritual leadership never sweeps reality under the rug. Before you can rebuild what is broken, you must have the courage to look at the rubble! You must look at the spiritual decay of the church, the moral collapse of our society, the doctrinal compromise in our pulpits, and say, \"This is broken. This is burned with fire.\" You cannot apply cosmetic band-aids to a cancer. You must inspect the wound before you can seek the cure.\n\nAnd notice verse 16: Nehemiah told no one—neither the priests, the nobles, nor the officials—what he was doing. Spiritual wisdom knows that there is a time to keep silent, and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Loose lips sink kingdom work before the foundation is even laid.\n\n---\n\n### IV. Mobilizing the Remnant for Holy Work (vv. 17–18)\n\nNow, in verse 17, having completed his diagnostic inspection and bathed the mission in prayer, Nehemiah gathers the Jewish leadership:\n\n**\"Then I said to them, 'You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision.'\"**\n\nListen to his appeal. \nFirst, he does not isolate himself. He doesn't say, \"You see the trouble *you* are in.\" He says, \"You see the trouble *we* are in.\" True spiritual leaders lead from within the flock, sharing the burden.\n\nSecond, he states the brutal reality: \"how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned.\" \n\nThird, he provides the ultimate motivation: \"that we may no longer suffer derision\"—that we may no longer be a *cherpah* [kher-PAW], a reproach, a disgrace! \n\nFolks, Nehemiah was not appealing to civic pride. He wasn't saying, \"Let’s make Jerusalem great again so we can boast in our architecture.\" He was saying, \"The holy name of Yahweh is being ridiculed among the pagans because our city lies in ashes! Let us build for the glory of God!\" The glory of God must be the burning engine of all Christian service.\n\nAnd then look at verse 18: **\"And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me.\"**\n\nNotice the order: first, he testified of *the hand of God*; second, he mentioned the words of the Persian king. Human authorization is secondary; divine providence is supreme! He shared with them how God had moved the emperor's heart, provided the timber, and granted safe passage. \n\nAnd what was the result? The people caught the fire! \n**\"And they said, 'Let us rise up and build.' So they strengthened their hands for the good work.\"**\n\nThe Hebrew verb for \"strengthened\" (*chazaq* [khah-ZAHQ]) means to bind up, fortify, make resolute. A dispirited, paralyzed remnant was suddenly transformed into a fearless construction army! Why? Because they saw that the living God was at work!\n\n---\n\n### V. Defiant Faith Against Worldly Intimidation (vv. 19–20)\n\nWhenever God’s people say, \"Let us rise up and build,\" Satan's minions immediately say, \"Let us rise up and destroy.\"\n\nLook at verse 19: **\"But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, 'What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?'\"**\n\nNow a third enemy joins the coalition: Geshem the Arab. Look at the geography, church! \nSanballat from the north in Samaria. \nTobiah from the east in Ammon. \nGeshem from the south in Arabia. \n\nIsrael was completely surrounded by hostile forces! And look at their tactics. \nFirst, they use *mockery*: they \"jeered at us\" (*vayyal'igu* [vay-yal-EE-goo]) and \"despised us\" (*vayyivzu* [vay-yiv-ZOO]). Satan always begins with ridicule. He tries to laugh the church out of her convictions. \n\nSecond, they use *slander and political intimidation*: \"Are you rebelling against the king?\" They play the sedition card! They accuse Nehemiah of treason against Artaxerxes.\n\nNow, how would you respond? If you were relying on your own flesh, you might pull out Artaxerxes’ letters with the royal seal and say, \"Look here! I have imperial permission! See this seal? The emperor authorized this!\"\n\nNehemiah doesn't even mention the king of Persia! Look at verse 20: \n**\"Then I replied to them, 'The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem.'\"**\n\nWhat a breathtaking response! Nehemiah doesn't hide behind Persian paperwork. He looks straight into the teeth of the enemy and invokes the supreme authority of the universe: **\"The God of heaven will make us prosper!\"** (*Elohei ha-shamayim hu yatzliach lanu* [el-o-HAY ha-shah-MAH-yim HOO yats-LEE-akh LAH-noo]). \n\nHe tells them, \"We don't take our marching orders from you, and we don't fear your threats. We are the servants of the God of heaven, and He will prosper our hands!\"\n\nAnd then he delivers an uncompromising line of spiritual demarcation: **\"but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem.\"**\n\nThe three words he uses are devastatingly precise:\n1. *Cheleq* [KHEH-leq]—\"portion,\" meaning an inherited share of the covenant land.\n2. *Tsedakah* [tsed-ah-QAH]—\"right,\" meaning legal jurisdiction or moral standing.\n3. *Zikkaron* [zik-kah-RONE]—\"claim\" or \"memorial,\" meaning a record of historical remembrance or worship in the holy city.\n\nNehemiah is declaring absolute ecclesiastical separation! He is telling these pagan syncretists, \"You have no part in this covenant. You have no legal standing before God. You have no right to meddle in the affairs of the church of Jesus Christ!\"\n\nChurch, this is a lesson modern evangelicalism desperately needs to hear. The church of Jesus Christ must never dilute her message, compromise her doctrine, or adopt the philosophies of the world in order to appease secular critics! We do not partner with the world to build the kingdom of God. As the Apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 6:14, \"What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?\"\n\n---\n\n### Conclusion and Appeal\n\nAs we step back from this powerful chapter, see how the hand of God works. \n\nGod places His servant in a position of influence. God breaks his heart over spiritual ruin. God prompts four months of agonized prayer. God gives him favor before the most powerful monarch on earth. God gives him wisdom to inspect the ruins in secret. God gives him courage to rally the people. And God gives him holy boldness to look into the sneering faces of the enemy and say, \"The God of heaven will make us prosper!\"\n\nAnd church, look past Nehemiah today and look to our Lord Jesus Christ. \n\nNehemiah was the royal cupbearer who risked his life before Artaxerxes.
